Monday. Imran's result came out, and Imran had missed the cut-off by a few marks. Jahnavi noticed Imran skip lunch and mute the group chat.

Wednesday. Jahnavi did not send advice. Jahnavi knocked on the door with two cups of tea. "I'm just here. No pep talk." Imran spoke for ten minutes, mostly about feeling behind everyone.

Saturday. Jahnavi offered one practical thing: "I'm going to the library. I can hold you a seat." Imran came and sat with a book, opening nothing. Later Jahnavi added quietly that if the heaviness did not lift over the coming weeks, talking with the college counsellor might help. Imran said, "Maybe."

qa.q: What did Jahnavi bring on Wednesday?
qa.a: Jahnavi brought two cups of tea.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been worried about while watching Imran skip lunch and mute the chat?
qa.a: That Imran was withdrawing and in pain, and unsure how to help without pushing.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do that helped more than advice would have?
qa.a: Offered company, listened, and offered small practical help such as holding a seat in the library.

qa.q: How might Imran have experienced Jahnavi's "No pep talk"?
qa.a: As a relief, allowing Imran to speak about feeling behind without being told to cheer up.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing withdrawal after a failure and offering company, listening and small help, with a gentle nudge toward a counsellor.

subtype: Friend who is struggling after failure [Observer]
passage: Asif, come here. I'm Aadhya, your Bua, and you're worried about your classmate who failed the entrance test, so let me tell you what I learned. When I was twenty-three my friend Sunil failed his exam for the second time. He stopped answering calls. I wrote him three long messages full of advice and got no reply. Then my mother said, "Go and sit with him." I went and said nothing clever. I brought vada pav, and we watched the street from his steps. After an hour he said, "I feel useless." I only nodded. Over the next weeks I carried his notebooks to the library and sat beside him. When he still could not sleep months later, I asked if he would try the college counsellor, and he did.

qa.q: What did Aadhya bring when going to sit with Sunil?
qa.a: Aadhya brought vada pav.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have been feeling when the three long messages got no reply?
qa.a: Worried and helpless, unsure how to reach Sunil.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Aadhya helped?
qa.a: Aadhya's mother said to go and sit with him, so Aadhya went and offered company instead of advice.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sunil when a friend simply sat beside him?
qa.a: Relieving, since it was after sitting with Aadhya for an hour that Sunil said "I feel useless".

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a friend who withdrew after failing, helped by company, small practical help and a nudge toward a counsellor.

passage:
The rain had flooded the lane outside Rafiq's building, so Varun waded the last fifty metres with a bag of food held above his head.
Rafiq's restaurant had closed a month ago. Since then he had stopped answering the group chat. Varun had noticed.
Rafiq opened the door in an old T-shirt. The flat smelled of stale air. He said, "Why did you come in this?"
"I brought biryani. And I had nothing else to do."
They ate on the floor because the power had gone. Varun didn't say "Everything happens for a reason" or "You'll bounce back." When Rafiq talked about the rent and the staff he'd let go, Varun just listened. When Rafiq went quiet, Varun washed the plates.
Before leaving, Varun said, carefully, "You've been in here a month, man. Would you talk to a counsellor? I'll find one and go with you, if you want."
Rafiq didn't answer. But he nodded, slowly.

qa.q: Why did Varun have to wade to Rafiq's building?
qa.a: The rain had flooded the lane outside Rafiq's building.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he watched Rafiq withdraw?
qa.a: Varun was worried about his friend, having noticed the silence in the group chat, and careful not to push too hard.

qa.q: Which of Varun's choices helped, and what did Varun avoid?
qa.a: He brought food, listened and washed the plates, avoided quick pep talks, and gently offered to find a counsellor and go along.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel when Varun offers to go with him to a counsellor?
qa.a: Rafiq might feel hesitant but cared for, which is why he doesn't answer at first but slowly nods.

grounding: An observer sees a friend withdrawing after his restaurant fails, offers company and listening rather than advice, and gently suggests professional support.

subtype: Friend who is struggling after failure [Observer]
passage:
Jagdish had shared the Mukherjee Nagar flat with Trisha for a year. When her civil services prelims result came and her name wasn't on it, he noticed the change within days.
She stopped cooking. She slept until noon, then sat by the window in the same kurta. Her books stayed stacked by the door.
Jagdish didn't lecture. He made two cups of tea each morning and left one by her. On Sunday he took her clothes to the laundry with his. One evening he sat on the floor near her and said, "Tell me about the paper, if you want." She talked for an hour. He mostly listened.
Three weeks later, nothing had shifted much. She still hardly went out.
One night he said gently, "Trisha, I think you should talk to someone who's trained for this. There's a counsellor at the university clinic. I'll come with you if you want."
She looked at him for a long moment. "Maybe Monday," she said.

qa.q: What did Jagdish leave by Trisha each morning?
qa.a: He made two cups of tea each morning and left one by her.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling after three weeks?
qa.a: Jagdish felt worried, because Trisha's withdrawal had lasted weeks and nothing had shifted much.

qa.q: Which of Jagdish's actions helped more than a pep talk would have?
qa.a: Small practical help like the tea and laundry, listening for an hour, and later gently suggesting a counsellor and offering to go with her.

qa.q: What might Trisha feel when Jagdish mentions the counsellor?
qa.a: Trisha might feel surprised and a little exposed, but also cared for, which is why she says "Maybe Monday."

grounding: Shows a flatmate who notices a friend withdrawing after exam failure, offers company and small help, and gently encourages professional support.

subtype: Friend who is struggling after failure [Observer]
passage:
"Jomon? It's Shankar. I'm outside."
"I didn't hear the bell."
"You didn't answer your phone for a week. So I came."
"I'm fine."
"Okay. Can I come in anyway?"
"…Fine."
"I brought parottas. You don't have to talk."
"The bar exam results came, you know."
"I know. I'm sorry, Jomon."
"Everyone keeps telling me I'll pass next time."
"I won't say that."
"Good."
"Do you want to talk about it or just eat?"
"Eat."
"Okay. Then eat. I'll do your dishes, the sink's full."
"You don't have to."
"I know."
"…Shankar? I haven't really left the flat since the results."
"Thank you for telling me. Will you walk with me to the chai stall tomorrow? Just ten minutes."
"Maybe."
"And if it still feels this heavy in a couple of weeks, will you let me help you find a counsellor? I'd come with you."
"…Okay."

qa.q: What food did Shankar bring?
qa.a: I brought parottas.

qa.q: How does Shankar seem to feel when Jomon admits not leaving the flat?
qa.a: Shankar seems concerned and grateful for the honesty, thanking Jomon and gently offering a small walk.

qa.q: What does Shankar do instead of giving quick advice?
qa.a: Shankar brings food, does the dishes, refuses to say "you'll pass next time," suggests a ten-minute walk and offers to help find a counsellor if it stays heavy.

qa.q: What is it like for Jomon when people keep promising a pass next time?
qa.a: Jomon finds it tiring and unhelpful, which is why Jomon says "Good" when Shankar won't say it.

grounding: An observer friend visits someone withdrawing after a failed exam, offers company and practical help, and gently points toward a counsellor.

subtype: Friend who is struggling after failure [Observer]
passage:
Last winter, after Darshan failed the civil services prelims for the third time, he went quiet. I, Binita, noticed it in small ways first: messages left on seen, his cricket kit gathering dust by my door where he'd dropped it, the lights off in his room when I walked past at seven.
I had a speech ready about many paths. I didn't give it. Instead I started turning up. I'd knock with two plates of rajma chawal and we'd eat and watch old matches. Some evenings he talked; most he didn't. Once I took his clothes to the laundry with mine. He said thanks as if it were a big thing.
After a month he was still sleeping till two and had skipped his cousin's wedding. So one night I said, gently, "I think talking to a counsellor might help. I'll sit with you while you book it, if you want." He was quiet a long time, then handed me his phone.

qa.q: What did Binita bring when knocking on Darshan's door?
qa.a: Two plates of rajma chawal.

qa.q: Why did Binita hold back the speech about many paths?
qa.a: Binita seems to have sensed Darshan was too hurt for a pep talk and cared more about simply being there, so Binita chose to keep turning up.

qa.q: What made Binita's suggestion about a counsellor gentle?
qa.a: Binita waited, spoke softly, and offered to sit alongside while Darshan booked it, making the step shared rather than a push.

qa.q: What might those evenings have meant to Darshan?
qa.a: For Darshan, quiet company and small help like the laundry probably felt like care without pressure, which is why a simple thanks sounded so big.

grounding: Shows a friend responding to someone withdrawing after failure with company and small help, then gently encouraging counselling.
